BST260 Final Project Proposal

Tongtong Gu

2026-11-18

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

To: BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026
From: Tongtong Gu
Subject: Proposal for Two Public Health Data Analyses

Project Overview

For my BST260 final project, I propose to develop an R package named finalproject and a public website using pkgdown. The project will include two reproducible Quarto vignettes that investigate distinct public health questions using datasets introduced in class. The first vignette will analyze the relationship between age and body mass index (BMI) among U.S. adults using NHANES. The second will examine temporal and geographic variation in homicide mortality rates using CDC data. Both analyses will emphasize data provenance, descriptive statistics, visualization, statistical modeling, and transparent discussion of limitations.

Vignette 1: Age and Body Mass Index Among U.S. Adults

Research question: How is age associated with BMI among U.S. adults, and does this association differ by sex?

Data source and provenance: The NHANES dataset available through the NHANES R package, based on the U.S. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey conducted by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). I will document the package version, source documentation, survey cycles represented, and relevant measurement definitions in the finished vignette.

Population and unit of analysis: Individual NHANES participants aged 20 years or older with eligible measurements. Each observation represents one participant.

Exposure: Age in years, initially treated as a continuous variable. I will consider flexible modeling of age if plots suggest a nonlinear association.

Outcome: BMI in kg/m², treated as a continuous variable. BMI is a descriptive anthropometric measure and is not interpreted as a direct measurement of body fat.

Prespecified covariates: Sex and race/ethnicity, selected based on their potential relationships with BMI and age distributions. Sex will also be evaluated as an effect modifier through an age-by-sex interaction. Missing values in the exposure, outcome, and covariates will be tabulated; a complete-case analysis will be used initially, with limitations of potential selection bias clearly stated.

Planned analyses: I will summarize participant characteristics, BMI distributions, and missingness; produce histograms, boxplots, and scatterplots or smoothed age–BMI curves; and fit linear regression models with age, sex, and race/ethnicity, including an age-by-sex interaction where appropriate. I will explore nonlinear associations if supported by the data. I will inspect whether the available survey design information permits design-appropriate weighted analysis; otherwise, I will describe unweighted results as sample-level exploratory findings, not nationally representative estimates.

Expected limitations: Cross-sectional data do not establish causal effects of age. Cohort effects, selection and nonresponse, measurement limitations, and potential confounding may affect interpretation.

Vignette 2: Geographic and Temporal Patterns in U.S. Homicide Mortality

Research question: How have homicide mortality rates changed over time across U.S. states, and how do these trends differ geographically?

Data source and provenance: The cdcmurd dataset provided in the BST260 finalproject template. Its package documentation describes homicide mortality rates by state and year for the 50 states and Washington, D.C., and links to the CDC National Center for Health Statistics state homicide statistics (https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/state-stats/deaths/homicide.html). I will verify the available years, rate definitions, units, data collection methods, and any suppression or missing values before analysis.

Population and unit of analysis: State-year observations for the 50 U.S. states and Washington, D.C., within the years represented by cdcmurd.

Exposure: Calendar year, modeled as a temporal variable. Geographic variation will be assessed using state and, where appropriate, Census region labels.

Outcome: State-level homicide mortality rate, treated as a continuous measure after verifying the dataset’s definition and units.

Prespecified covariates and comparisons: State or region will be considered to describe persistent geographic differences in rates. I will examine whether the direction and magnitude of temporal patterns vary by geographic area. Missing or suppressed state-year values will be identified and reported rather than assumed to be zero.

Planned analyses: I will inspect the dataset structure and completeness, summarize the distribution of rates across states and years, visualize national and regional descriptive trends, and compare state-specific trajectories. Subject to data coverage and variable definitions, I will fit descriptive regression models with year and state/region terms and consider interactions to explore geographic differences in trends. If age adjustment or population weighting is not supported by the available data, I will explicitly limit interpretation accordingly.

Expected limitations: These are ecological observations and cannot establish individual-level risk factors or causal effects. Trends can be affected by coding changes, variation in population structure, suppression, and the choice of mortality rate definition.

Reproducibility, Deliverables, and Reporting

The repository at https://github.com/tongtong24x/finalproject will contain a valid R package, two source Quarto vignettes, code used to create descriptive statistics and visualizations, source citations, and a pkgdown website published through GitHub Pages at https://tongtong24x.github.io/finalproject/. I will check package installation and site generation and document the steps needed to reproduce the analyses.

Each vignette will include its investigative objectives, data provenance and variable definitions, data-cleaning choices, descriptive findings, visualizations and models, a scientific interpretation of results, and limitations. I will write reusable R functions where they improve consistency in data summaries and figures. The findings will be reported only after the datasets have been examined; no results are assumed in this proposal.
